posts.text: This is the first national assessment of the Trump administration's ICE surge on labor markets, published May 4 by NBER. The underlying data is the federal Current Population Survey. Read Chloe East's work, it's careful, non-partisan, and important:  nber.org/papers/w35129?utm_c…
What the data can't yet tell us: long-run effects. East flags that labor contraction could reduce supply and drive up prices for goods like housing and manufactured products.

The ratio East finds: for every 6 male undocumented workers lost, the labor market also loses 1 U.S.-born male worker. In a region with 1,200 ICE arrests, that projects to roughly 1,200 fewer U.S.-born men employed.

The construction sector saw twice the average impact: a 3% employment drop for U.S.-born men with a high school degree or less. In construction, 13% of workers are undocumented. When labor disappears, employers take on less work, not more U.S. workers.
For U.S.-born workers, there was no wage increase, no measurable increase in job opportunities. In fact, employment among U.S.-born men with a high school degree or less fell 1.3% in surge regions.

CU Boulder economist Chloe East compared regions with large, sudden ICE arrest increases (Jan–Oct 2025) to those without. Employment among remaining likely-undocumented immigrants fell 4% on average,  a chilling effect, not a removal effect.
New NBER research asks a simple question: does an ICE enforcement surge create jobs for U.S.-born workers? The answer, based on federal labor data across 58 regions, is no.
Full series, including Eileen Grench and Lam Thuy Vo's investigation of the November arrests and a printable rights guide for residents: documentedny.com/2026/04/27/…

@documentedny spent three months on the ground in Queens, interviewing residents, organizers, and officials, to document what this enforcement looks like at street level. That reporting matters alongside the FOIA data.

What the data still can't tell us: how many stops had any legal basis at all. Sighting data tracks ICE presence, not legal predicate. That gap is exactly what the April 9 EDNY lawsuit is trying to close.

Elmhurst, Corona, and Jackson Heights, the neighborhoods at the center of this enforcement surge, are up to 70% foreign-born. That density and the enforcement concentration within it are not unrelated.

Of those 811 collateral arrests, 85% involved people with no criminal history. Even among targeted arrests, 73% had no criminal conviction or pending charges. That's ICE's own data, obtained via FOIA.
THE CITY's April 2 analysis of Deportation Data Project FOIA data found that 1 in 4 ICE arrests in NYC (Aug. 2025–Mar. 10, 2026) were "collateral", people who were not the intended target.
On one street corner in Corona, Queens, ICE arrested 7 men in a single afternoon last November. That block-level story connects to a national pattern worth understanding.

Full reporting from The Independent: independent.co.uk/news/world… 

 For more on ICE detention conditions and what the data does and doesn't show, my Substack: austinkocher.substack.com

I want to be careful here: I can document what happened to Lothirath specifically. What I can't tell you from available data is whether ICE's medical protocols changed in response, or whether similar cases are being flagged internally. That gap in transparency is itself a story.

What the data doesn't yet tell us: how many people with serious medical conditions are currently in ICE detention aren't receiving care. ICE held 73,000 people as of mid-Jan. 2026, up more than 75% since Jan. 2025. Medical infrastructure has not kept pace.

ICE's own data shows 32 detainees died in custody in 2025, the deadliest year since 2004. Reports indicate 32 of 46 deaths between Jan. 2025–Mar. 2026 were people with preexisting conditions whose health deteriorated in detention.

When he finally got home to Minnesota, he was hospitalized immediately, missing two more chemotherapy sessions. A subsequent scan showed the cancer had spread to his bone marrow. Source: Minnesota Star Tribune reporting, March–April 2026.

He was transferred to El Paso and held in a tent facility with roughly 60 other detainees. ICE released him only after his caregiver presented a hospital letter stating he would "succumb" without treatment. He was too weak to travel for days after release.
